import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1071

*References:*
* [erdosproblems.com/1071](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1071)
* [Da85] Danzer, L., _Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry_.
  Intuitive geometry (Siófok, 1985), 167-177.
-/

open Set Metric EuclideanGeometry Order

namespace Erdos1071

/-- Two segments are disjoint if they only intersect at their endpoints (if at all). -/
def SegmentsDisjoint (seg1 seg2 : ℝ² × ℝ²) : Prop :=
  segment ℝ seg1.1 seg1.2 ∩ segment ℝ seg2.1 seg2.2 ⊆ {seg1.1, seg1.2, seg2.1, seg2.2}

/--
Can a finite set of disjoint unit segments in a unit square be maximal?
Solved affirmatively by [Da85], who gave an explicit construction.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle and ChatGPT.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos1071.lean"]
theorem erdos_1071.parts.i :
    answer(True) ↔ ∃ S : Finset (ℝ² × ℝ²),
      Maximal (fun T : Finset (ℝ² × ℝ²) =>
        (∀ seg ∈ T, dist seg.1 seg.2 = 1 ∧
          seg.1 0 ∈ Icc 0 1 ∧ seg.1 1 ∈ Icc 0 1 ∧
          seg.2 0 ∈ Icc 0 1 ∧ seg.2 1 ∈ Icc 0 1) ∧
          (T : Set (ℝ² × ℝ²)).Pairwise SegmentsDisjoint) S := by
  sorry

/-- Is there a region $R$ with a maximal set of disjoint unit line segments that is countably infinite?
Solved affirmatively by [Fo99], who gave an explicit construction.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle and ChatGPT.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos1071b.lean"]
theorem erdos_1071.parts.ii :
    answer(True) ↔ ∃ (R : Set ℝ²) (S : Set (ℝ² × ℝ²)),
      IsOpen R ∧ IsConnected R ∧ S.Countable ∧ S.Infinite ∧
      Maximal (fun T : Set (ℝ² × ℝ²) =>
        (∀ seg ∈ T, dist seg.1 seg.2 = 1 ∧ seg.1 ∈ R ∧ seg.2 ∈ R) ∧
        T.Pairwise SegmentsDisjoint) S := by
  sorry

end Erdos1071

findings.description: The predicate under `Maximal` checks `seg.1 ∈ R ∧ seg.2 ∈ R`, rather than requiring the unit segment itself to lie in R. These conditions are not equivalent for the permitted open, connected regions. For example, let R be the punctured plane and take endpoints (-1/2, 0) and (1/2, 0). Lean verifies that R is open and connected, the endpoints belong to R, and their distance is 1, but their open segment contains the missing origin. Conversely, an open unit diameter lies in the open ball of radius 1/2 although neither endpoint belongs to that ball. Thus the predicate changes both the admissible families and the competitors used to define maximality.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/1071 defines the unit segments as rotated and translated copies of `(0,1)` and asks for a maximal family in a region R. Erdős, Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry (1987), §7, pp.173–174, says: 'Let R be any region and let there be given in R a maximal set of disjoint unit intervals.' https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1987-27.pdf
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `dist seg.1 seg.2 = 1 ∧ seg.1 ∈ R ∧ seg.2 ∈ R` with `dist seg.1 seg.2 = 1 ∧ openSegment ℝ seg.1 seg.2 ⊆ R`. The existing `SegmentsDisjoint` relation can be retained: at unit length it is equivalent to disjointness of the open segments.

findings.description: The bibliography attributes 'Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry', pp.167–177, to Danzer under `[Da85]`. This is Erdős's 1987 paper reporting Danzer's construction, not a paper authored by Danzer.
findings.source_evidence: The source's bibliography identifies `[Er87b] Erdős, P., Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry. Intuitive geometry (Siófok, 1985) (1987), 167–177`: https://www.erdosproblems.com/bibs/Er87b. The paper itself names P. Erdős as author and credits Danzer with the example in §7: https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1987-27.pdf.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the bibliographic entry with the correct `[Er87b]` citation. Change the part (i) docstring to credit Danzer's construction 'as reported in [Er87b]'.

findings.description: The asserted construction is attributed to `[Fo99]`, but that reference is not identified anywhere in the file. It is also absent from the cited problem page, which instead documents Alexeev's construction. This is an unresolved provenance/reference defect; it is not evidence against the affirmative answer.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/1071 says 'Alexeev has proved in the comments that the unit square itself admits a countably infinite maximal such set.' The construction appears in Alexeev's 25 January 2026 comment at https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1071, with its formal proof linked on 30 January. Neither the file nor the cited page supplies a bibliographic entry for `[Fo99]`.
findings.suggested_fix: Cite Alexeev's documented construction, or supply a complete, checkable reference for `[Fo99]` if a different earlier construction was intended.

reformulations.difference: The source uses disjoint open segments, whereas Lean tests whether the intersection of the corresponding closed segments is contained in the union of their four endpoints.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For nondegenerate segments, a point of a closed segment belongs to its open segment exactly when it is neither endpoint. Consequently an intersection point lies in both open segments exactly when it is none of the four endpoints. Both theorems require distance 1, so their segments are nondegenerate. The equivalence with `Disjoint (openSegment ℝ s.1 s.2) (openSegment ℝ t.1 t.2)` was proved in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean. This encodes the source's main open-segment question, not its separately mentioned stricter closed-segment variant.

reformulations.difference: Maximality is expressed on `Finset` families, rather than among arbitrary families of segments.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The property of being a family of admissible pairwise disjoint segments is hereditary under subsets. Any proper admissible extension of a finite family contains one new segment, whose insertion already gives a finite proper admissible extension. Hence maximality among finite families is equivalent to maximality among all families. A general Lean equivalence for hereditary predicates was proved in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean.

reformulations.difference: Containment in the unit square is checked only at the endpoints.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Unlike the arbitrary region in part (ii), the closed unit square is convex and closed. Endpoint membership implies containment of the entire segment by convexity. Conversely, containment of the open segment implies endpoint membership because its closure is the closed segment and the square is closed. This equivalence was proved for the exact coordinate-defined square in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean.
